why_angle: The roundups shoppers find give panel-size tiers and a generic 20–50 mA parked-car drain. One even says a 2.4–5 W panel covers that drain. Go Power! gives generic 10W/20W Ah/day by region but names no kits and gives no prices. None works out a named kit's winter Ah/day against that drain or what each Ah/day costs. This page shows that 10 W kits fall short in a northern winter (1.04 Ah/day against up to 1.2 Ah/day of drain) and that the VEVOR 20W costs least per Ah/day ($16.78). No Dealectric product is a solar maintainer. VEVOR is on Amazon (B0FPWMFF6B) but is listed here at its maker price, because the angle's figure is based on price.

page.answer: Short answer. A 12 volt solar trickle charger keeps up if its daily charge beats the battery's drain. In a northern winter a 10W maintainer makes 1.04 Ah/day against up to 1.2 Ah/day of parked-car drain. Buy 20W: the VEVOR 20W (MPPT charge controller) makes 2.08 Ah/day at $16.78 per Ah/day.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Winter charge per day. Go Power!'s method: panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.7 (flat-panel loss) ÷ 12.8 V. Using 1.9 winter sun-hours for the Great Lakes and Northeast: 20 × 1.9 × 0.7 ÷ 12.8 = 2.08 Ah/day. A 10 W panel gives 1.04, 12 W gives 1.25, 30 W gives 3.12 and 50 W gives 5.20.
  • What a parked car takes. Energy For The Taking puts a parked car's drain at 20–50 mA. 0.050 A × 24 h = 1.2 Ah/day, and 0.020 A × 24 h = 0.48 Ah/day.
  • Margin. 2.08 ÷ 1.2 = 1.7×, so a 20 W kit covers a 50 mA drain with room for cloudy days. 1.04 ÷ 1.2 = 0.87×, so a 10 W kit loses ground in a northern winter.
  • Cost per Ah/day. Maker price ÷ winter Ah/day. VEVOR 20W: 34.90 ÷ 2.08 = $16.78. SUNER BC-20W Ultra: 85.95 ÷ 2.08 = $41.32.
  • Current ceiling. Panel watts ÷ 12 V: 20 ÷ 12 = 1.67 A. OptiMate rates its DUO 20W at exactly this, 1.67 A average, with 3–5 A only as short pulses. SUNER and VEVOR publish no amp rating, so treat 1.67 A as the most any 20 W kit can deliver.

How much a solar trickle charger really puts back

A panel's rating is its output in full sun. A winter day in the north gives only about 1.9 hours' worth of that, and a panel lying flat loses roughly 30% more. That is why the table counts amp-hours per day rather than watts. Zelpio's test (published 2 October 2026) backs up the 0.7 factor. With a solar panel tester, a SUNER 20W Pro measured 14.75 W in sun (74% of its rating) and 7.33 W lying flat under cloud (37%).

The controller matters as much as the panel. In the same Zelpio test, some 20 W maintainers kept charging past 15.5 V on a battery that was already full. Every kit in the table has a 3-stage or automatic controller that stops when the battery is full. OptiMate is the only maker here that publishes the controller's night-time draw, under 0.5 mA, which is 0.012 Ah/day. It also starts charging a battery from as low as 4 V. For a lithium battery, note what Go Power! says: LiFePO4 must not be charged below freezing, and its BMS blocks charging when the cells are cold. In midwinter, a lithium battery in a cold car may only take charge on warm afternoons. SUNER's Ultra models need you to switch them to Lithium mode by hand. VEVOR lists LiFePO4 among its supported battery types.

One caveat on the pick: on the VEVOR page, the main listing shows In Stock, but the 20 W option in one selector shows Out of Stock. Check the box before you pay. VEVOR lists IP65 and a 0–60° bracket.

Not recommended

SUNER BC-20W Solar Battery Charger Ultra. At $85.95 it costs more than SUNER's own BC-30W-Ultra PRO ($69.99), which has the same three charging modes and 50% more panel. It also costs $26 more than the BC-20W-Ultra PRO ($59.95), which has the same 20 W. Any 10 W kit for a car stored up north: it makes 1.04 Ah/day against up to 1.2 Ah/day of drain, so the battery still drops.
